nodes.name: Nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: \barr{ll} u_t-\Delta\beta(u)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)u)=0\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rr^d),\vsp u(0,x)=u_0(x), \earr

nodes.name: Hypothesis (i)
nodes.statement: $\beta(0)=0$, $\b\in C^1(\rr)$, and \begin{equation} \g_0|r_1-r_2|^2\le(\b(r_1)-\b(r_2))(r_1-r_2),\ r_1,r_2\in\rr, \end{equation} where $0<\g_0<\9.$
nodes.statement_short: $\beta(0)=0$, $\beta\in C^1$ and $\beta$ is strongly monotone with constant $\gamma_0>0$.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii)
nodes.statement: $b\in C_b(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd)$, $b(x, \cdot) \in C^1(\rrd; \rrd)$ $ \forall x\in\rrd$ {\it such that} $$\mbox{$\sup\{|b^i_r(x,r)|;x\in\rrd,i=1,2,$ $|r|\le M\}\le C_M,$ $\ff M>0.$}$$
nodes.statement_short: $b$ is bounded continuous, $C^1$ in $r$, with $b_r$ bounded on bounded $r$-sets.

nodes.name: Hypothesis (ii')
nodes.statement: $b(x,0)=0$ $\forall x\in\rrd$, $b \in C^1(\mathbb R^{d+1}; \rrd) $ {\it and for $$\delta(r):=\sup\{|b_x(x,r)|;\ x\in\rrd\},$$we have} $\delta\in C_b(\rr).$
nodes.statement_short: $b(x,0)=0$, $b\in C^1$ and $\delta(r)=\sup_x|b_x(x,r)|$ is bounded continuous.

nodes.name: Component and derivative notation for $b$
nodes.statement: Here$$b(x,u)=\{b^i(x,u)\}^d_{i=1}\mbox{ and }b^i_r=\frac{\pp b^i}{\pp r}, b_x=\big\{ \nabla_x \, b^i(x, \cdot) \big\}_{i=1}^d.$$

nodes.name: Notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u$
nodes.statement: In the following, we shall use the notation $b^*(x,u)=b(x,u)u.$

nodes.name: Existence of mild solutions (Barbu--Röckner)
nodes.statement: if (i)--(ii) hold and, in addition, for $\Phi(u)\equiv\frac{\beta(u)}u,$ $u\in\rr,$ we have $\Phi\in C^2(\rr)$, then there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii) and $\Phi=\beta(u)/u\in C^2$, (1.1) has a mild solution in $C([0,\infty);L^1)$ for every $u_0\in L^1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Barbu & Röckner, From nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations to solutions of distribution dependent SDE [1]
conclusions: there is a mild solution $u\in C([0,\9);L^1(\rr^d))$ for each $u_0\in L^1(\rr^d)$

nodes.name: Mild solution
nodes.statement: The mild solution $u$ is defined~as $$u(t)=\lim_{h\to0}u_h(t)\mbox{ in }L^1(\rr^d),\ \ff t\ge0,$$where \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mild solution is the $L^1$-limit of the piecewise-constant implicit Euler approximations $u_h$ of (1.1).

nodes.name: Implicit finite-difference scheme (1.6)
nodes.statement: \barr{l} u_h(t)=u^i_h\mbox{ for }t\in[ih,(i+h)h],\ i=0,1,...,Nh=T,\vsp u^{i+1}_h-h\D\b(u^{i+1}_h)+h\,{\rm div}(b(x,u^{i+1}_h)u^{i+1}_h)=u^i_h\mbox{ in }\cald'(\rr^d),\\\hfill i=0,1,...,\vsp u^0_h=u_0.\earr
nodes.label: e1.6

nodes.name: Nonexpansive semigroup of mild solutions
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$.
conclusions: $S(t)u_0=u(t),\ t\ge0,$ is a strongly continuous semigroup of nonexpansive mappings in $L^1(\rrd)$

nodes.name: Mild solutions are distributional solutions
nodes.statement: As easily seen, any mild solution is a distributional solution but the uniqueness follows in the class of mild solutions only.

nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE (1.7)
nodes.statement: dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt+\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{\b(u(t,X(t))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t).

nodes.name: $L^p$ spaces and norms $|\cdot|_p$
nodes.statement: Denote by $L^p(\rr^d)=L^p$ the space of $p$-summable functions on $L^p$, with the norm denoted $|\cdot|_p$.

nodes.name: Sobolev spaces $H^k$, $H^{-k}$ and the space $C_b$
nodes.statement: By $H^k(\rrd)=H^k$, $k=1,2$, and $H^{-k}(\rrd)=H^{-k},$ we denote the standard Sobolev spaces on $\rrd$ and by $C_b(\rrd)$ the space of continuous and bounded functions on $\rrd$.

nodes.name: Spaces $C^k$ and $C^1_b$
nodes.statement: By $C^k(\rrd)$ we denote the space of continuously differentiable functions on $\rrd$ of order $k$, by $C^1_b(\rrd)$ the space $\left\{u\in C^1(\rrd);\frac{\pp u}{\pp y}\in C_b(\rrd),\ j=1,...,d\right\}.$ The spaces of continuous and differentiable functions on $(0,T)\times\rrd$ are denoted in a similar way and we shall simply write $$C^1_b(\rrd)=C^1_b,\ C^k(\rrd)=C^k,\ k=1,2.$$

nodes.name: $L^2$ scalar product and $H^1$--$H^{-1}$ pairing
nodes.statement: The scalar product in $L^2$ is denoted $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2$ and by ${}_{H^{-1}}\!\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{H^1}$ the pairing between $H^1$ and $H^{-1}.$ Of course, on $L^2\times L^2$ this coincides with $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_2.$

nodes.name: $H^{-1}$ scalar product and norm
nodes.statement: The~scalar product $\<\cdot,\cdot\>_{-1}$ on $H\1$ is taken~as \begin{equation} \<u,v\>_{-1}=\<(I-\D)\1u,v\>_2,\ \ff u,v\in H\1 \end{equation}with the corresponding norm \begin{equation} |u|_{-1}=(\<u,u\>_{-1})^{\frac12},\ u\in H\1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\langle u,v\rangle_{-1}=\langle (I-\Delta)^{-1}u,v\rangle_2$ on $H^{-1}$, with norm $|u|_{-1}$.

nodes.name: Spaces of Schwartz distributions $\mathcal{D}'$
nodes.statement: By $\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)$ and $\cald'(\rrd)$ we denote the space of Schwartz distributions on $(0,\9)\times\rrd$ and $\rrd$, respectively.

nodes.name: Sobolev space $W^{1,2}([0,T];\mathcal{X})$
nodes.statement: If $\calx$ is a Banach space, we denote by $W^{1,2}([0,T];\calx)$ the infinite dimensional Sobolev space $\{y\in L^2(0,T;\calx);$ $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;\calx)\}$, where $\frac d{dt}$ is taken in the sense of vectorial distributions.

nodes.name: Partial derivative notation $z_r$, $z_x$
nodes.statement: We also set, for each $z\in C^1(\rrd\times\rr)$, $$z_r(x,r)=\frac\pp{\pp r}\ z(x,r),\ \ z_x=\nabla_x z(x,r).$$

nodes.name: Common norm symbol $|\cdot|$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement: We shall denote the norms on $\rrd$ and $\rr$ by the same symbol $|\cdot|$.

nodes.name: Brezis--Crandall uniqueness for $b\equiv0$
nodes.statement: In the special case $b\equiv0$, such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established earlier in \cite{3} for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$.
assumptions: for continuous and monotonically nondecreasing functions $\b$
conclusions: such a uniqueness result for\eqref{e1.1} was established earlier in \cite{3}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of distributional solutions
nodes.statement: Let $T>0$ and let conditions {\rm(i)--(ii)} on $\beta$ and $b$ hold. For each $u_0\in L^\9\cap L^1$, the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under (i)--(ii), the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation (1.1) has at most one bounded, integrable distributional solution.
conclusions: the \FP\ equation \eqref{e1.1} has at most one distributional solution \begin{equation} u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd). \end{equation}
nodes.label: t1

nodes.name: Solution class $L^1\cap L^\infty$
nodes.statement: u\in L^1((0,T);L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd).
nodes.label: add-e5

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$) It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$ Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$ Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.) Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation} Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation} We note that \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation} We also have \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}This yields \begin{equation} \barr{ll} |\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} \le\b_M|u|_2|u|_{-1} \earr\end{equation}and \begin{equation} \barr{l} \left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vsp \qquad\le 2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vsp \qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1}, \earr \end{equation} where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and $$\barr{lcl} \b_M&=&\dd\sup\{\b'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vsp b_M&=&\dd\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in\rrd,\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vsp&\le& \sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in\rrd\} < \infty \earr$$ by (ii). By \eqref{e2.3}--\eqref{e2.7}, we get $$\barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_{2} \le(\b_M+2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9) |u(t)|^{}_2|u(t)|^{}_{-1},\\\hfill\mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$ This yields $$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\ff t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed. To conclude the proof, we shall prove
nodes.statement_short: Subtract two solutions, apply $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$ and derive an $H^{-1}$ energy inequality from strong monotonicity; Gronwall gives $u\equiv0$, given the regularity of Claim 2.2.

nodes.name: Difference of two solutions
nodes.statement: Let $u_1,u_2\in L^1(0,T;L^1)\cap L^\9((0,T)\times\rrd)$ be two distributional solutions to \eqref{e1.1} and let $u=u_1-u_2.$ We have \begin{equation} \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr \end{equation} (Here, $b^*(x,r)=b(x,r)r,\ \ff x\in\rrd,\ r\in\rr.$)
nodes.statement_short: Take two solutions and write the equation (2.1) for their difference $u$.

nodes.name: Equation for the difference $u=u_1-u_2$ (2.1)
nodes.statement: \barr{l} u_t-\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0\\\hfill\mbox{ in }\cald'((0,\9)\times\rrd)\vsp u(0,x)=0.\earr
nodes.label: e2.1

nodes.name: Regularity of the difference
nodes.statement: It should be mentioned that, by (i), (ii), it follows that $u_i,\beta(u_i), b^*(\cdot, u_i)\in L^2((0,T);L^2),$ $i=1,2$, and, therefore, $u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-2}).$

nodes.name: Introduce $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$and note that $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism of $H\1$ onto $H^1$ and $\Gamma\in L(H^{-2},L^2).$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the isomorphism $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}:H^{-1}\to H^1$.

nodes.name: Operator $\Gamma=(1-\Delta)^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Gamma:H\1\to H^1$ defined by $$\Gamma u=(1-\D)^{-1}u,\ u\in H\1(\rrd)$$

nodes.name: Equation for $y=\Gamma u$
nodes.statement: Since $u_i\in L^2(0,T;L^2),$ $i=1,2,$ it follows that $y=\Gamma u\in L^2(0,T;H^2)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];L^2)$ and so, by~\eqref{e2.1}, we have \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr \end{equation} where $\frac{dy}{dt}\in L^2(0,T;L^2).$ (We note that here $\frac{dy}{dt}$ is taken in the sense of $L^2$-valued vectorial distributions on $(0,T)$ and so $y:[0,T]\to L^2$ is absolutely continuous.)
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\Gamma$ to (2.1) to get the $L^2$-valued equation (2.2) for $y=\Gamma u$.

nodes.name: Equation for $y=\Gamma u$ (2.2)
nodes.statement: \barr{l} \dd\frac{dy}{dt}-\Gamma\D(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2))+\Gamma\,{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2))=0,\\\hfill\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\\ y(0)=0,\earr
nodes.label: e2.2

nodes.name: Extra regularity assumption
nodes.statement: Assume first that, in addition, \begin{equation} u\in L^2(0,T;H^1);\ u\in W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: First assume the extra regularity (add-e6); it is removed by Claim 2.2.

nodes.name: Energy identity
nodes.statement: Now, we take the scalar product in $L^2$ of \eqref{e2.2} with $u=u_1-u_2$. Taking into account that $$\<\frac{du}{dt}\,(t),u(t)\>_{-1}=\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}, \mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$we get, by \eqref{e2.2} that $$\barr{l} \dd\frac 12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_2 =\<\Gamma(\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2\vsp \qquad-\<\Gamma\,{\rm div}((b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_2,\ \mbox{a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr$$
nodes.statement_short: Test (2.2) with $u$ to obtain an $H^{-1}$ energy identity.

nodes.name: Use strong monotonicity
nodes.statement: By \eqref{e1.2}, this yields for a.e.~$t\in(0,T)$ \begin{equation} \barr{r} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|u(t)|^2_2 \le\<\b(u_1(t))-\b(u_2(t)),u_1(t)-u_2(t)\>_{-1}\vsp \qquad-\<{\rm div}(b^*(x,u_1(t))-b^*(x,u_2(t))),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}.\earr \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Strong monotonicity (1.2) gives the energy inequality (2.3).

nodes.name: Auxiliary inequalities
nodes.statement: We note that \begin{equation} |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2. \end{equation} We also have \begin{equation} |{\rm div}\,F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2,\ \ff F\in (L^2)^d. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Record $|\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2$ and $|{\rm div}F|_{-1}\le2|F|_2$.

nodes.name: Contractivity of $\Gamma$ in $L^2$ (2.4)
nodes.statement: |\Gamma f|_2\le|f|_2,\ \ff f\in L^2.
nodes.label: e2.4

nodes.name: Bound diffusion and drift terms
nodes.statement: This yields \begin{equation} \barr{ll} |\<\b(u_1)-\b(u_2),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}| \le|\b(u_1)-\b(u_2)|_{2}|u|_{-1} \le\b_M|u|_2|u|_{-1} \earr\end{equation}and \begin{equation} \barr{l} \left|\<{\rm div}\ (b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)),u_1-u_2\>_{-1}\right|\vsp \qquad\le 2|b^*(x,u_1)-b^*(x,u_2)|_2|u_1-u_2|_{-1}\vsp \qquad\le2(|b|_\9+b_M|u_1|_\9)|u|_2|u|_{-1}, \earr \end{equation} where $M=\max\{|u_1|_\9,|u_2|_\9)$ and $$\barr{lcl} \b_M&=&\dd\sup\{\b'(r);\ |r|\le M\},\vsp b_M&=&\dd\sup\left\{\frac{|b(x,u_1)-b(x,u_2)|}{|r_1-r_2|};\ x\in\rrd,\ |r_1|,|r_2|<M\right\}\vsp&\le& \sup\{|b_r(x,r)|;|r|\le M,\ x\in\rrd\} < \infty \earr$$ by (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Bound the two right-hand terms of (2.3) by $|u|_2|u|_{-1}$ with constants from (ii).

nodes.name: Combined energy inequality
nodes.statement_short: Combine (2.3)--(2.7) into one differential inequality.

nodes.name: Gronwall conclusion
nodes.statement: This yields $$\frac d{dt}\,|u(t)|^2_{-1}\le C|u(t)|^2_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).$$Since $u:[0,T]\to H^{-1}$ is absolutely continuous and narrowly continuous, we infer that $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, $\ff t\in[0,T]$, and so $u\equiv0$, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Absorb terms and apply Gronwall to get $|u(t)|_{-1}=0$, hence $u\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Reduce to Claim 2.2
nodes.statement: To conclude the proof, we shall prove
nodes.statement_short: It remains to prove the regularity Claim 2.2.

nodes.name: Regularity of bounded distributional solutions
nodes.statement: If $u$ is a distributional solution to \eqref{e1.1} satisfying \eqref{add-e5}, then \eqref{add-e6} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Every distributional solution of (1.1) in $L^1\cap L^\infty$ lies in $L^2(0,T;H^1)\cap W^{1,2}([0,T];H^{-1})$.
assumptions: $u$ is a distributional solution to \eqref{e1.1} satisfying \eqref{add-e5}
nodes.label: add-l1

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2.2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: We shall proceed as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}. Namely, we set $v_1-v_2=v$ for two solutions $v_1,v_2$ of \eqref{e3.2} By a similar argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{t1}, we may assume that $v$ satisfies \eqref{add-e6}. Then we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} v_t-\D(\Psi v)+{\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0,\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),\vsp v(0)=0.\earr \end{equation} For $y=\Gamma v$, we get \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac d{dt}\ y-\Gamma\D(\Psi v)+\Gamma\ {\rm div}(b(x,u)v)=0\vsp y(0)=0\earr \end{equation} and multiplying scalarly in $L^2$ with $v$, as above we get that \begin{equation} \barr{l} \dd\frac12\ \frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}+\g_0|v(t)|^2_2 \le(|\Psi|_\9+|b|_\9)|v(t)|^{}_2|v(t)|^{}_{-1},\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T).\earr \end{equation} This yields $$\frac d{dt}\ |v(t)|^2_{-1}\le|v(t)|^2_{-1}\mbox{ a.e. }t\in(0,T),$$ and, therefore, $v\equiv0$, as claimed.

nodes.name: McKean--Vlasov SDE
nodes.statement: Consider for $T\in(0,\9)$ and $u_0\in L^1\cap L^\9$ the McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation (SDE) \begin{equation} \barr{l} dX(t)=b(X(t),u(t,X(t)))dt +\dd\frac1{\sqrt{2}}\(\frac{\b(u(t,X(t)))}{u(t,X(t))}\)^{\frac12}dW(t),\vsp \hfill 0\le t\le T,\\ u(0,\cdot)=\xi_0,\earr\end{equation}on $\rrd$. Here, $W(t),\ t\ge0,$ is an $(\calf_t)$-Brownian motion on a probability space $(\Omega,\calf,\mathbb{P})$ with normal filtration $\calf_t$, $t\ge0,$ $\xi_0:\Omega\to\rrd$ is $\calf_0$-measurable such that $$\mathbb{P}\circ\xi^{-1}_0(dx)=u_0(x)dx,$$ and $u(t,x)=\frac{d\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}}{dx}\,(x)$ is the Lebesgue density of the marginal law $\mathcal{L}_{X(t)}=\mathbb{P}\circ X(t)\1$ of the solution process $X(t)$, $t\ge0$.
